processing: As with other Yunnan raw pu-erh, the leaf is typically wilted, wok-fired, rolled and sun-dried into mao cha, then sold loose or steamed and pressed; no ripe-style pile fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as is usual for Mengku raw pu-erh; little is documented about the season here beyond that.
appearance_dry: Dark, shiny dried leaf, which locals call big black leaves.
appearance_liquor: Bright and brilliant, typically golden when young.
appearance_wet: Thick large leaves in dark olive, as with other Mengku raw teas.
taste_profile: A rich, full-flavoured raw tea; beyond that, little has been recorded, though Mengku tea in general is sweet, fragrant and vigorous.

brewing.notes: Short early steeps; this is a strong style, and it rewards patience more than force.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, mainly as spring tea, with two clear price tiers: one published list gives old-tree leaf at several times large-tree leaf. Young cakes are the usual purchase. Ask for tree age and which part of the village it came from.
description:
Dahusai sits on Mengku's western half-mountain, a village of Lahu and Han households near Xiaohusai and under the Bangma Snow Mountain. It has less fame than Bingdao, but it holds one of the town's largest concentrations of old tea trees, and the trade wants it for its rich taste.

Its mao cha looks different from its western neighbours: dark and shiny after drying, called big black leaves by the people of Mengku. There are many small primary workshops in the village, and the method is the usual raw pu-erh one.

Expect a bright liquor and a rich taste. Detailed tasting records are few, so judge a sample by its body, its sweetness after the swallow, and how long it stays interesting. Short steeps first.

The best-preserved old garden, some 50 to 60 mu, lies in the Lahu riverside part of the village; most of the trees over 200 years old are here, and they have not been dwarfed. Only some of what is sold as Dahusai can come from there, so price and tree age should match. The Sanjiacun and Tofu village gardens are often counted with the area too.
history:
Dahusai was Mengku's main tea-producing village in 1949, and in the 1950s Shuangjiang County marked it as a key tea-growing area, with planting every year after.

A 2014 cooperative and the Fenghua tea factory's contract farming have tied the village more closely to the market in recent years; a 2021 report counted 126 primary workshops here.
